## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{0}{100}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why does an agent that can search everything it has ever stored still act on the wrong facts?_

An agent's tasks can span days: a repository it must come back to, a user whose preferences it should not ask for twice, a lesson from a failed attempt it should not repeat. Information needed later remains outside the active model call, in source systems, observation logs, search indexes, and notes the agent writes for itself. Persistence alone does not make that information useful. An index can lag the file just edited, a mistaken diagnosis can return as a confident lesson, and an old preference can survive after the user changes it. A similarity score says that a record resembles a query, not that it is current, permitted, or true. The engineering problem is therefore not storing more. It is deciding what should persist, how a later task obtains appropriate evidence, and how corrections and deletion change what can return. In H·S·A terms, durable State carries the consequences of these decisions beyond one session, requiring explicit ownership of what is retained and how it influences a continuing horizon.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Classify persistent records by their source, evidential role, and relationship to derived search representations
- Specify a retrieval contract that bounds access, returned content, resource use, and required freshness
- Compare pre-staged retrieval with model-directed search under common task and resource constraints
- Select retrieval methods for an information need and estimate multi-hop evidence against a serialized-token budget
- Design a memory write policy for admission, correction, supersession, expiry, and deletion
- Explain version-aware exclusion and fallback without mistaking removal of stale candidates for complete fresh retrieval
- Evaluate cross-session memory policies by task outcomes, update behavior, and total resource cost

:::

## What Should Persist {#sec-vol3-persistent-need}

The connection-pool repair may resume after the current session ends. The next session needs the candidate source at `r18`, the earlier failure at `r17`, the subsequent result of `test_waiter_notified_on_return`, and the broader checks that remain unresolved. These records do different jobs. The source identifies what the repository contains; the test result reports what happened under particular conditions; the progress note tells the next session where to continue. Keeping only the final message can lose the supporting evidence. Keeping every message without its scope can turn the earlier failure into an apparent failure of the new candidate.

The previous chapters separated the information selected for a call from the attention computation retained by the serving system. Context selection does not require forgetting everything outside the request, and KV state need not disappear at a session boundary. KV may remain available or be serialized, but its reuse still concerns compatible computation. This chapter concerns information that should influence a later decision: what to retain, how to retrieve it, and how to change it when its source or intended use changes. Storage medium alone does not distinguish these responsibilities.

### Persistent records have different roles

Most persistent information the agent uses already exists outside its own trajectory, such as a repository, database, or configuration. Some is produced by the work, including observations, summaries, and proposed lessons. Treating all of these as undifferentiated “agent memory” conceals the distinction between a claim and its support. @Tbl-vol3-memory-tiers separates the roles before considering how to search them.

| **Record role**          | **Example**                                                                                    | **What a later use must preserve**                                                        |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Source record            | `src/pool.py` at a specified revision; the user's stated scheduling preference                 | The designated source, applicable version or scope, and access conditions                 |
| Observation or event log | The outcome of `test_waiter_notified_on_return` under recorded source, test, and configuration | What was observed, when, and under which conditions; gaps in the retained history         |
| Agent-written memory     | A progress note, session summary, or proposed repair lesson                                    | Supporting records, uncertainty, intended scope, and the policy for correction or removal |
| Derived retrieval index  | Search entries over source files, logs, or notes                                               | Which source generation produced the entry and how changes affect its use                 |

: **Roles of persistent records**: These are roles in an evidence chain, not a hierarchy of storage devices or universal levels of trust. One record can serve more than one role. {#tbl-vol3-memory-tiers tbl-colwidths="[23,33,44]"}

A source-of-record is the designated evidence source for a particular claim. The repository is the source for the file's contents at a revision; a recorded user statement can be the source for that user's preference. Neither designation makes every statement in the record true or gives its contents instruction authority. A repository may contain a bug, and a comment may contain an instruction the task never authorized. The principle that authority stays with the source (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}) preserves the relationship between a claim and its source; it does not make source content a permission grant.

Observations preserve what the system saw. The failed check at `r17` remains useful history after `r18` is written, while the later pass supports only the selected reproducer under the conditions recorded. A log can be the primary evidence that a particular response was observed without proving everything the response claims. It also preserves only what its recording and retention policy captured. A log held in process memory and a committed durable record have different failure boundaries; @sec-vol3-durable-execution develops the persistence and recovery contract.

Agent-written memory reorganizes such information for later use. A progress note can name pending checks; a summary can shorten a long investigation; a proposed lesson can suggest what to inspect next time. These records can save repeated work, but the transformation can also lose qualifications or invent a cause. “The targeted reproducer passed at `r18`” is supported by the recorded result. “Connection-pool timeouts are always caused by missed notifications” is a broader claim the result does not establish. Storing that claim does not improve its evidence.

A retrieval index changes how records are found. It may store exact text, search terms, embeddings, or links between records. Some representations lose detail and some preserve the complete payload, but neither a high rank nor exact copying establishes that the result applies to the present task. Indexes may cover source records, observations, and agent-written notes alike. Their contents need not form a static reference library, and placing a note in a searchable store does not itself update the model's weights.

### Reads and writes share a lifecycle

Return to the repair after `r18` has been written. A search index built from `r17` can still return the old `src/pool.py`. If the result is presented as current source, the model may infer that the patch failed and propose a duplicate edit. The old excerpt is not necessarily false: it describes the wrong revision for that decision. The applicability rule from @sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot now extends beyond the prompt to the retained copies from which future prompts are assembled.

Indexing introduces both a benefit and an obligation. Precomputed search representations can avoid repeatedly scanning or transforming the source, but changes may require new entries and withdrawal of obsolete ones. Waiting for that work can delay a read or write; doing it in the background requires a policy for requests that arrive before it finishes. Direct source reads remain an option when they are authorized and affordable. An index earns its maintenance cost only when it improves the workload's retrieval policy; every task does not need every index.

Writes matter even when no file is being repaired. Suppose a user explicitly says “no meetings before 10,” then later replaces it with “no meetings before 11” for the same scheduling scope. The second statement is nearly identical in wording but changes what the assistant should do. A novelty filter that discards similar records would lose the update. Retaining both as equally current would leave the next session with a conflict the user already resolved. The memory policy must distinguish creating a record from superseding it and must carry the change to the representations used for retrieval. The user's calendar and time-zone scope remain part of interpreting either preference.

The full write path also decides when a record needs revalidation, when it expires, and how deletion withdraws it and its derived copies from future use. These are not properties supplied by a similarity metric. They require a record lifecycle alongside the read policy. The later write section develops that lifecycle; first, retrieval needs an interface that makes its scope and limitations visible. Whether the runtime stages evidence in advance or the model proposes a search, the returned material must fit the call's budget and identify what was obtained, from where, and with what completion status.

## The Retrieval Contract {#sec-vol3-persistent-governance}

The connection-pool repair needs the current implementation of `src/pool.py` and the evidence associated with `test_waiter_notified_on_return`. A search can return both an r17 failure and an r18 reproducer pass. Both records may be useful, but they answer different questions. Before choosing a search method, we need to specify what the next decision requires and what a returned result establishes.

::: {#dfn-episodic-retrieval-contract .callout-definition title="Retrieval contract"}

A **retrieval contract**\index{Retrieval contract!definition} specifies the information requested, the permitted scope and resource limits of the read, and the provenance, applicability, and completion information returned with its results.

**Significance**: It makes a bounded search result interpretable before that result enters the next model call.

**Distinction**: Ranking identifies candidates under a search rule. The contract separately governs access, versions, returned content, and what the search did or did not complete.

**Common pitfall**: Treating an empty or truncated response as proof that the requested information does not exist.

:::

The contract applies to an indexed search, a database lookup, and a direct file read. It does not require every request to pass through several indexes or a relevance-score threshold. Its purpose is to connect an information need to an observation the agent can use without inventing guarantees that the retrieval did not supply.

### The bounded request {#sec-vol3-persistent-query-tuple}

An information need such as “find the notification logic” leaves several choices open. The caller may need the current workspace, an earlier revision, or a comparison. The request must also identify the permitted repository and how much evidence the next invocation can accept. @Tbl-vol3-query-tuple separates these decisions from the choice of index.

| Request field                    | Meaning in the repair task                                                                 | Boundary it establishes                                                               |
|:---------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Query or information need        | Locate the waiter-notification implementation or the recorded reproducer result            | The requested match or observation, not a promise that it exists                      |
| Authorized scope and principal   | The designated repair workspace and the identity under which it is read                    | The runtime checks permitted paths and records; a scope string alone grants no access |
| Version or freshness requirement | Read r18, compare r17 with r18, or read the current source under stated snapshot semantics | Which state can answer the question                                                   |
| Result-count and payload limits  | Bound returned items and their serialized representation                                   | Count and content size are separate limits                                            |
| Execution limits                 | Deadline and supported bounds on scans, expansions, or other search work                   | When to stop waiting or searching and report incomplete work                          |
| Optional filters                 | Restrict file type, symbol kind, or other relevant metadata                                | Narrow the information need without replacing authorization                           |

: **A bounded retrieval request**: The runtime can supply task-wide defaults, while each query specializes the information need within those limits. {#tbl-vol3-query-tuple}

A version requirement is more precise than “recent.” An r17 index entry is unsuitable as current r18 source even if it was indexed moments ago. An age limit can trigger a refresh, including in systems that also receive change events, but cannot prove that a younger record is unchanged. If the service cannot meet the requested version, it can attempt an authorized direct read or return an explicit incomplete outcome. Excluding old candidates does not make the new version appear in an unfinished index; @sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation develops that maintenance problem.

Result-count limits protect one part of the interface. Ten returned files could contain far more text than ten short excerpts, and returning one item could still require searching a large corpus. The payload limit bounds what reaches the caller; search-work limits bound what the service spends finding it. A deadline bounds the caller's wait according to the service contract. If cancellation has not stopped backend work, that work remains outstanding rather than disappearing from the task's resource accounting.

### The result envelope {#sec-vol3-persistent-result-envelope}

A usable response describes the search as well as its records. At the response level, report the scope and version actually searched, completion status, and any limitation that affects interpretation. `complete` means the declared search operation completed under its stated semantics; it does not mean every relevant fact was found. `partial` identifies a limited response, with a reason such as a deadline, unavailable source subset, or output cap. `unavailable` means the service could not supply a usable response. Where supported, a continuation cursor lets a later bounded request obtain more material.

These statuses must agree with the operation. A completed approximate search may still miss the true nearest neighbors. A completed literal scan with no matches establishes absence of that literal only within the scanned scope and version. A partial scan with no matches establishes neither. If a response contains only a selected page of a larger result, it should expose that selection and continuation rather than silently imply exhaustion.

Each returned item carries its content together with a source identifier, relevant range or record key, source version, and provenance. An observation also needs the conditions it describes: the r18 test result names the source and test revisions, selected check, configuration, and outcome. A derived lesson identifies its supporting records and its status as an inference. An optional retrieval score names the method that produced it; scores from different methods need not share a scale or represent probabilities.

For the repair, an envelope might identify a source excerpt as `src/pool.py`, revision `r18`, and a particular function range. Another identifies a failure log as an observation of `r17`. The latter can explain why the investigation began without establishing that the candidate still fails. This is the same applicability distinction used in the context manifest, now preserved across the durable read boundary.

A content hash can help check whether the returned bytes match a recorded version under the hash scheme's assumptions. It does not authenticate the author, establish that a claim is true, or authorize an action. Likewise, labeling a record as repository source or agent-written memory helps identify its role without making its instructions privileged. If a later edit depends on an unchanged version, the tool must enforce an appropriate action-time precondition; a successful earlier read does not close the interval in which another writer can change the file.

### Staging bounded evidence {#sec-vol3-persistent-quarantine}

The retrieval response is not automatically the next prompt. The runtime selects evidence for the pending decision, preserves the source and version labels needed to interpret it, and measures the final serialized request. This applies Context Engineering's working-set decision at the read boundary. Candidate generation may examine more records than the model ultimately sees.

Returned text remains data, including text from a local repository. Serialization should distinguish the payload from runtime instructions and escape syntax according to the chosen format. Provenance labels and delimiters help interpretation; neither guarantees that the model will ignore an instruction embedded in the payload. Access controls and policy-appropriate redaction constrain what may be exposed, while authorization of later actions remains a separate boundary. The security treatment develops those controls rather than assuming a wrapper makes retrieved material harmless.

Payload accounting must include wrappers, source identifiers, version labels, and status information, not just the record bodies. The following hypothetical ledger shows how that changes the number of complete records that fit. Its counts stipulate one serialization, not a universal relationship between characters, fields, and model tokens.

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-retrieval-payload-ledger
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SERIALIZED RETRIEVAL PAYLOAD LEDGER
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-06-retrieval-payload-ledger
# │ Goal: Bound complete retrieved records after output and envelope reserves.
# │ Show: Retrieval allowance, record capacity, payload used, and remainder.
# │ How: Explicit hypothetical token counts; no hardware or tokenizer claim.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_math

class RetrievalPayloadLedger:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario assumptions, in serialized tokens) ─────────────
    capacity = 32_768
    output_reserve = 2_048
    other_input = 24_576
    envelope = 128
    body = 512
    metadata = 64

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    allowance = capacity - output_reserve - other_input
    record = body + metadata
    records = (allowance - envelope) // record
    used = envelope + records * record
    remaining = allowance - used

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(allowance == 6_144, "retrieval allowance")
    check(record == 576 and records == 10, "complete record capacity")
    check(used == 5_888 and remaining == 256, "complete serialized payload")
    check(used <= allowance < used + record, "one additional record cannot fit")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    capacity_str = fmt_int(capacity)
    output_reserve_str = fmt_int(output_reserve)
    other_input_str = fmt_int(other_input)
    envelope_str = fmt_int(envelope)
    body_str = fmt_int(body)
    metadata_str = fmt_int(metadata)
    record_str = fmt_int(record)
    records_str = fmt_int(records)
    remaining_str = fmt_int(remaining)
    allowance_math = fmt_math(rf"{capacity:,} - {output_reserve:,} - {other_input:,} = {allowance:,}")
    payload_math = fmt_math(rf"{envelope} + {records} \times {record} = {used:,}")
```

::: {#nbk-06-retrieval-payload-ledger .callout-notebook title="Making room for retrieved evidence"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical call permits `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.capacity_str` tokens in total. Reserve `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.output_reserve_str` for output; all other serialized input occupies `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.other_input_str`. How many complete retrieval records fit?

**Math**: The retrieval allowance is `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.allowance_math` tokens. Stipulate a `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.envelope_str`-token response envelope and records consisting of `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.body_str` body tokens plus `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.metadata_str` metadata tokens, or `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.record_str` tokens per record.

The largest complete-record count is `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.records_str`. Those records and their envelope consume `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.payload_math` tokens, leaving `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.remaining_str` tokens, too little for another complete record.

**Systems insight**: A body-only top-count limit can admit more evidence than the call can serialize. Reserve output and metadata first, then select content. This packing bound says nothing about whether the chosen records answer the question or how long retrieval takes.

:::

Actual token counts must be measured after serialization with the intended model interface; independently tokenized fragments need not add up exactly. If a relevant record does not fit, the runtime can choose a smaller coherent excerpt, defer it to a later read, or return a handle with an explicit omitted-content status. An excerpt retains enough scope to show what was selected and what remains unavailable. A handle is a route to a future read, not evidence already present in this call.

::: {#chk-06-retrieval-contract .callout-checkpoint title="Interpreting a bounded result"}

- [ ] A query for current source returns an r17 excerpt after the workspace reaches r18. What historical use remains valid, and what must happen before using it to plan an r18 edit?
- [ ] A search reaches its deadline with no matches. How should its status differ from a completed literal scan of the requested snapshot?
- [ ] A set of record bodies fits the retrieval allowance before provenance is added. What must the runtime measure before dispatching the model call?

:::

## Agentic Retrieval {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-agentic-retrieval}

Two retrieval policies can begin the connection-pool repair. One runtime pre-stages the relevant source, test, and earlier failure before asking the model for a next step. Another gives the model bounded text search, file reading, and symbol-navigation tools. The model finds the notification logic, reads the corresponding test, and follows references when the first result leaves an open question. Both use the same retrieval contract; they differ in when the information need is refined and who proposes the next query.

Pre-staging applies the retrieval-augmented generation pattern of supplying external material with a model request [@lewis2020retrieval]. **Agentic retrieval**\index{Agentic retrieval!definition} lets the model propose searches during the execution loop, interleaving retrieved observations with further reasoning [@yao2023react]. These are combinable choices, not separate kinds of storage. A runtime can pre-stage results from several queries or a structural traversal, and a model-directed probe can use a direct read or an index.

Pre-staging is useful when the next decision's evidence requirements are already known. Supplying `src/pool.py` and `tests/test_pool.py` can avoid a model round spent merely locating those files. It can also stage irrelevant material or miss a dependency that only becomes apparent after inspection. Iterative search lets a result change the next query: a test name reveals a helper, or a source reference identifies another file. That opportunity does not guarantee better queries. The model can pursue an unhelpful lead, repeatedly search the same region, or stop before obtaining the needed evidence.

A live-source baseline is important before adding an index. A bounded text search and direct read can inspect the designated workspace without waiting for a separate search index to catch up. If the task already identifies the path or literal, this may be all the retrieval machinery it needs. The returned bytes describe the read's observed version or snapshot, not a guarantee that the workspace will remain unchanged. Separate file reads need not form one consistent repository snapshot. Literal matching also does not determine which occurrence is the relevant definition or prove that all semantic dependencies have been found.

An index earns its maintenance cost when it improves the task's retrieval policy: reducing repeated scan work, helping with vocabulary mismatch, or making useful relationships easier to follow. The comparison includes index construction and refresh, not just query latency. Direct search cost depends on the selected corpus, filtering, and storage behavior; it is not automatically too slow because the repository is large.

@Tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-staged-vs-agentic summarizes the policy choice. A probe is not necessarily a separate model call: one call can propose independent searches that the runtime batches or runs concurrently. Dependent probes must wait for the observations they need. Returned material then enters the ordinary context-selection policy rather than remaining in every later prompt forever.

| Property               | Runtime pre-staging                                   | Model-directed probing                                                 |
|:-----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Query selection        | Runtime policy selects evidence for the upcoming call | Model proposes a query using the available observations                |
| Useful when            | Likely evidence needs are known in advance            | Results reveal which question to ask next                              |
| Additional work        | Retrieval and staging before the call                 | Search work and any additional model rounds needed to refine the query |
| Characteristic failure | Missing dependencies or unnecessary material staged   | Unproductive exploration or premature stopping                         |
| Freshness              | Determined by source, version, and read contract      | Determined by the same contract, not by model involvement              |
| Limits                 | Retrieval and call budgets                            | The same budgets plus trajectory-wide stopping limits                  |

: **Pre-staging and model-directed retrieval**: Query timing and ownership change, while source applicability and runtime-enforced limits remain shared. {#tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-staged-vs-agentic}

The runtime retains control of authority and budgets in both designs. A model can propose a narrower path, query string, or filter; it cannot expand the authorized workspace, change the principal, or raise resource ceilings. The tool schema communicates the supported request fields, while the result communicates limits and continuation options. Tool Calling develops those interfaces in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-schemas and @sec-vol3-tool-calling-streaming.

A combined policy can pre-stage a compact workspace outline and let subsequent probes retrieve the details. Cross-session memory follows the same pattern: stage an applicable user preference when the task requires it, and expose other records through bounded search. Whether that reduces total work must be measured against the extra staged tokens and searches it avoids. Once the information need and retrieval boundary are clear, the next choice is the matching method: exact lookup, lexical ranking, or structural navigation.

## Structured Retrieval {#sec-vol3-persistent-bm25}

The retrieval contract bounds a request; the next decision is which method can answer it. In the connection-pool repair, locating `tests/test_pool.py`, finding references to `test_waiter_notified_on_return`, and identifying the function enclosing a suspicious statement are different information needs. A known path supports a direct read. An identifier supports literal search or symbol lookup. A description of the failure may require ranking several candidates before the agent knows which source to inspect. These methods can be useful independently; the runtime does not need to deploy every index before supporting a repair.

### Exact lookup and lexical ranking

An exact path lookup asks for a named object within the authorized repository and version. A literal text search asks where a specified character sequence occurs under declared matching rules. Neither identifies the meaning of every occurrence: the test identifier might appear in a definition, a comment, or a stored failure log. When the agent already knows the file and version it needs, reading that source is a useful baseline against which to justify an index.

An *inverted index* supports repeated lexical searches by mapping each indexed term to a postings list of documents containing it. A posting can record a document identifier, term frequency, and positions. The index's analyzer determines what counts as a term, including whether it preserves a whole identifier, splits `snake_case`, folds case, or applies stemming. Consequently, a ranked match for an analyzed identifier is not necessarily an exact match for the original string. An exact-match field or a check against the returned source can establish that narrower property.

When several documents match, ranking determines which candidates enter the bounded result. BM25 combines term rarity, diminishing returns from repeated occurrences, and document-length normalization [@robertson2009bm25]. One common form is

$$
\operatorname{score}(d,Q)=\sum_{q\in Q}\operatorname{IDF}(q)
\frac{f(q,d)(k_1+1)}{f(q,d)+k_1(1-b+b|d|/\overline{\ell})},
\qquad
\operatorname{IDF}(q)=\ln\left(1+\frac{N-n(q)+0.5}{n(q)+0.5}\right).
$$

Here $Q$ contains the query terms, $d$ is an indexed document, $f(q,d)$ is a term's frequency in that document, $|d|$ is its length in analyzer terms, and $\overline{\ell}$ is the collection's mean document length. The collection contains $N$ documents, of which $n(q)$ contain term $q$. These lengths are not the foundation model's token counts. The parameter $k_1>0$ controls frequency saturation; at fixed length, the frequency factor approaches $k_1+1$ as frequency grows. The parameter $b\in[0,1]$ controls length normalization, with $b=0$ disabling it. Document boundaries, analyzer choices, and parameter settings therefore affect ranking even when the underlying source text is unchanged.

```{python}
#| label: ltm-bm25-ranking-calc
#| echo: false
# What: Compare two lexical candidates, not their correctness.
# How: Apply the displayed BM25 variant to a hypothetical one-term query.
from math import log
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_ratio

class BM25Ranking:
    # 1. LOAD — stipulated corpus statistics, not measured repository data.
    documents = 100_000
    matching_documents = 5
    average_length = 400
    short_length, long_length = 80, 4_000
    short_frequency, long_frequency = 1, 6
    k1, b = 1.2, 0.75

    # 2. EXECUTE — lengths and frequencies are analyzer-term counts.
    idf = log(1 + (documents - matching_documents + 0.5) / (matching_documents + 0.5))
    short_normalizer = k1 * (1 - b + b * short_length / average_length)
    long_normalizer = k1 * (1 - b + b * long_length / average_length)
    short_score = idf * short_frequency * (k1 + 1) / (short_frequency + short_normalizer)
    long_score = idf * long_frequency * (k1 + 1) / (long_frequency + long_normalizer)

    # 3. GUARD — validate the scenario and the ordering being illustrated.
    check(0 < matching_documents <= documents, "Document frequencies must be valid")
    check(0 < short_frequency <= short_length, "Short-document counts must be valid")
    check(0 < long_frequency <= long_length, "Long-document counts must be valid")
    check(average_length > 0 and k1 > 0 and 0 <= b <= 1, "BM25 parameters must be valid")
    check(short_score > long_score > 0, "The example must rank the short candidate first")

    # 4. OUTPUT — presentation values for all displayed scenario quantities.
    documents_str = fmt_int(documents)
    matching_documents_str = fmt_int(matching_documents)
    average_length_str = fmt_int(average_length)
    short_length_str, long_length_str = fmt_int(short_length), fmt_int(long_length)
    short_frequency_str, long_frequency_str = fmt_int(short_frequency), fmt_int(long_frequency)
    k1_str, b_str = fmt_ratio(k1, precision=1), fmt_ratio(b, precision=2)
    idf_str = fmt_ratio(idf, precision=3)
    short_score_str = fmt_ratio(short_score, precision=2)
    long_score_str = fmt_ratio(long_score, precision=2)
```

::: {#exmp-06-quantitative-bm25-score-dynamics-on .callout-example title="A higher lexical score is a ranking decision"}
**Scenario.** Consider a hypothetical index of `{python} BM25Ranking.documents_str` documents with a mean length of `{python} BM25Ranking.average_length_str` analyzer terms. A single query term appears in `{python} BM25Ranking.matching_documents_str` documents. With $k_1=$ `{python} BM25Ranking.k1_str` and $b=$ `{python} BM25Ranking.b_str`, its inverse document frequency is `{python} BM25Ranking.idf_str`.

**Analysis.** A short candidate contains `{python} BM25Ranking.short_length_str` terms and `{python} BM25Ranking.short_frequency_str` occurrence of the query term; a long candidate contains `{python} BM25Ranking.long_length_str` terms and `{python} BM25Ranking.long_frequency_str` occurrences. Substituting these counts into the scoring rule gives `{python} BM25Ranking.short_score_str` for the short candidate and `{python} BM25Ranking.long_score_str` for the long candidate. Repetition alone does not determine their order: saturation and length normalization outweigh the long candidate's additional occurrences.

**Systems lesson.** The short candidate is ranked higher, not established as the correct definition or sufficient evidence. If it is a comment while the long candidate contains the implementation, the agent still needs source inspection or structural information. Choosing whole files rather than functions as documents can also change the scores. Ranking must be evaluated for the information needs it is intended to serve.
:::

### Structural evidence

Lexical matches identify text occurrences. Structural retrieval can distinguish the enclosing function, a declaration, and an identifier used in an expression. A parser provides a syntax tree and source spans; symbol resolution or a separate semantic analysis can add relationships between definitions and references. Those are distinct capabilities. Parsing a call expression does not by itself determine every implementation that might execute.

In the repair, a structural query could return the function containing a notification call in `src/pool.py`, allowing the agent to read a meaningful unit instead of an arbitrary fragment. A supported reference query could then identify callers for further inspection. Its coverage depends on the language, available dependencies, build configuration, and analysis. Dynamic dispatch, reflection, generated code, and cross-process calls may require additional information. A missing edge is therefore not proof that no dependency exists, and a static call edge is not an observation that the call executed.

@Tbl-vol3-lexical-vs-ast-table separates the questions these methods answer. Lexical indexes can carry path, language, and symbol metadata; the distinction is not that lexical search lacks all scope information, but that text matching alone does not establish a semantic relationship.

| **Information need**                              | **Suitable starting method**                      | **What the result establishes**                                                    |
|:--------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Read a known path or locate a literal identifier  | Direct source read or declared exact-match search | The requested content or occurrences within the searched scope and version         |
| Find likely relevant documents from query terms   | Lexical ranking such as BM25                      | Candidate order under the analyzer, document boundaries, and scoring rule          |
| Find an enclosing function or resolved references | Syntax or semantic index with declared coverage   | Parsed boundaries or analysis-derived relationships, not complete runtime behavior |

: **Exact, Lexical, and Structural Retrieval**: Choose the method according to the information required, then interpret its result within the method's coverage. {#tbl-vol3-lexical-vs-ast-table}

### Scope before interpretation

All three methods operate within the earlier retrieval contract. Searching the approved repository at r18 is not interchangeable with finding a high-scoring r17 record. In the repair, restricting an initial probe to `src/pool.py` and `tests/test_pool.py` can focus the evidence, provided the result reports that limited scope. A subsequent probe may need to expand it to investigate callers. The chosen scope is a search decision, not a claim that other files cannot matter.

Filtering and ranking also interact. If a service first selects its highest-ranked candidates globally and only then discards candidates outside the requested paths, it can return an empty set even though eligible matches exist farther down the ranking. Restricting candidates before selecting the final ranked set avoids this particular loss; continued search after filtering is another option. Access checks remain mandatory regardless of the ranking strategy. If work limits prevent further search, the service must report the corresponding coverage or partial result, rather than letting the agent interpret an empty list as proof of absence.

### When the vocabulary is unknown

Exact and structural lookup are strongest when the agent already has useful names or locations. Earlier in the investigation, it may know only the symptom: “a connection is returned, but another caller keeps waiting.” The implementation might express the relevant operation through `notify_all`, without using the same phrasing. This is the vocabulary mismatch problem [@furnas1987vocabulary]. Its effect depends on the analyzer and the surrounding text: identifier splitting, synonym expansion, or query reformulation may recover useful lexical matches. Once the test identifier is known, a literal lookup can be more direct than another conceptual search.

When those approaches do not produce adequate candidates, dense retrieval offers another way to relate a description to differently worded source material. It is an optional response to the information need, not a required successor to every lexical query. The next section examines what that representation adds and how to combine candidate rankings without treating semantic similarity as verification.

## Hybrid Retrieval {#sec-vol3-persistent-dense-retrieval}

The repair agent may know the exact identifier `test_waiter_notified_on_return`, or it may know only the symptom: "a connection is returned, but another caller keeps waiting." These are different retrieval problems. Lexical retrieval can exploit the identifier directly. For the symptom, useful records may discuss notification or blocked waiters without repeating the query's words. Query reformulation and lexical expansion can bridge some of this gap. Dense retrieval supplies another candidate-generation method, using learned representations to match a query with potentially relevant records.

### Matching beyond shared words

A dense retriever encodes a query and each searchable record as vectors. In a bi-encoder design, records can be encoded before a request arrives; the runtime encodes the query and compares it with those stored vectors [@karpukhin2020dense]. This moves record-encoding work out of the query path, but not out of the system. New or changed records need corresponding representations, and changing the encoder can require rebuilding an index.

The comparison rule belongs to the encoder and index configuration. Dot product is one common rule. Cosine similarity divides the dot product by the vectors' lengths; it equals the dot product when both vectors have unit length. A system should not normalize representations merely because another retriever does so. Neither score is, by itself, a calibrated probability that a record answers the question.

For the repair task, a dense retriever might connect the waiting symptom to the return-and-notify implementation. That is a candidate worth inspecting, not proof of a defect. It might also prefer a passage about a different kind of waiting. Conversely, an exact identifier can be distinctive to lexical retrieval without being well represented by an embedding model. The useful question is which method finds the evidence this workload needs, within the retrieval contract's limits.

### Choosing the search work

An exact vector scan scores every vector in the eligible search set under the chosen metric. It provides a useful reference for measuring what an approximate search misses. It can also be a reasonable serving method when that set is small enough. Authorization and version constraints still apply: fast matching against an unauthorized repository or an obsolete snapshot does not satisfy the request.

The scan's basic resource requirements are visible without choosing a particular machine. Let $N$ be the number of eligible vectors, $d$ their dimension, and $b$ their bytes per component. Reading each stored component once requires $Ndb$ bytes. Using the conventional count of two floating-point operations per multiply-add, dot-product scoring requires approximately $2Nd$ FLOPs. These counts exclude query encoding, candidate selection, and fetching the records themselves.

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-memory-bandwidth-and-latency-floor
#| echo: false
# What: Establish the data volume and arithmetic of an illustrative exact scan.
# How: Count vector components; do not assume a hardware latency or throughput.
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_FP16, GB, GFLOP, byte, flop
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_flops, fmt_int, fmt_memory

class VectorScanLatencyFloor:
    # LOAD: Hypothetical corpus; representation width is a shared constant.
    n_vectors = 10_000_000
    d_dim = 768
    bytes_per_val = BYTES_FP16

    # EXECUTE: Raw vector bytes and multiply-add work, excluding other stages.
    footprint = n_vectors * d_dim * bytes_per_val
    flops_total = 2 * n_vectors * d_dim * flop

    # GUARD: Preserve the intended teaching magnitudes and dimensional units.
    check(abs(footprint.to(GB).magnitude - 15.36) < 1e-9, "vector bytes")
    check(abs(flops_total.to(GFLOP).magnitude - 15.36) < 1e-9, "scan FLOPs")

    # OUTPUT: All computed prose quantities use the shared formatter.
    n_vectors_str = fmt_int(n_vectors)
    d_dim_str = fmt_int(d_dim)
    width_str = fmt_memory(bytes_per_val, unit=byte, precision=0)
    footprint_str = fmt_memory(footprint, unit=GB, precision=2)
    work_str = fmt_flops(flops_total, unit=GFLOP, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-06-memory-bandwidth-and-latency-floor .callout-notebook title="The work of an exact vector scan"}
**Problem.** Consider a hypothetical searchable set of `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.n_vectors_str` vectors, each with `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.d_dim_str` components stored in FP16 at `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.width_str` per component. How much data and arithmetic does one exact dot-product scan require?

**Math.** Multiply the vector count by the dimension and component width:

$$
Ndb = 10^7 \times 768 \times 2\ \text{bytes}.
$$

The raw vectors occupy `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.footprint_str`. Counting two FLOPs per multiply-add gives $2Nd = 2 \times 10^7 \times 768$ FLOPs, or `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.work_str` per scan. These are vector-storage and scoring estimates, not the total index footprint or complete request cost.

**Systems insight.** Search-set size controls both costs linearly. A narrower eligible set reduces the scan work; a larger one may make an approximate index attractive. The byte count alone cannot determine latency. That also depends on where the vectors reside, the available bandwidth and arithmetic throughput, batching, and other work sharing the machine.
:::

Approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search avoids scoring every vector, at the risk of missing some of the highest-scoring vectors under the metric. For example, a hierarchical navigable small-world (HNSW) index follows links among vectors and spends a configurable amount of work exploring candidates [@malkov2018efficient]. More exploration generally offers a different work–recall trade-off; it is not a universal latency or recall guarantee. Graph links consume storage beyond the vectors themselves. Other approaches partition the search space or compress vector representations, trading search coverage or score fidelity against work and storage.

These choices must be evaluated on the eligible records and query types the agent actually uses. Recall against an exact vector scan measures agreement with that metric's nearest neighbors, not whether the neighbors contain adequate evidence. An ANN operation can complete under its declared search semantics without finding every exact neighbor. If the operation instead stops at a deadline or cannot access part of the requested scope, the retrieval result must expose that limitation through the contract's status and coverage fields. Neither outcome establishes that a missing fact is absent from the source of record.

### Combining candidate rankings

Hybrid retrieval uses more than one matching method, such as lexical and dense retrieval, to generate candidates. Before combining lists, the runtime must establish candidate identity. Here, identity includes repository or tenant scope, source path, version, and span where relevant. A passage from revision `r17` must not merge with its changed `r18` counterpart just because their paths or text are similar. Identical text in another tenant is not the same authorized evidence.

Lexical scores and dense scores need not share a scale. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)\index{Reciprocal rank fusion} combines their ranked lists rather than adding the raw scores [@cormack2009reciprocal]. Let $L_m$ be the list returned by method $m$, and $r_m(x)$ the one-based rank of candidate $x$ in that list. For a positive smoothing parameter $k$, the truncated-list convention used here is

$$
\operatorname{RRF}(x) = \sum_{m:\,x\in L_m} \frac{1}{k + r_m(x)}.
$$ {#eq-vol3-reciprocal-rank-fusion}

A candidate absent from a list contributes zero for that list. Increasing $k$ reduces the relative difference between contributions from nearby ranks; it does not make the method parameter-free.[^fn-rrf-rank-monotonicity] The runtime must also specify how it breaks ties and how many candidates each method supplies.

[^fn-rrf-rank-monotonicity]: **RRF score monotonicity**\index{Reciprocal rank fusion}: With fixed $k > 0$, moving an item from rank $r$ to $r' < r$ in one input list increases its contribution by $1/(k+r')-1/(k+r)>0$ [@cormack2009reciprocal]. If its contributions from other lists do not decrease, its total score increases. This is a property of the item's score, not a guarantee of improved final rank when other candidates also change, or of relevant evidence.

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-reciprocal-rank-fusion
#| echo: false
# What: Reproduce an explicitly hypothetical pair of truncated candidate lists.
# How: Sum exact reciprocal ranks, then break score ties by stable candidate ID.
from fractions import Fraction
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_ratio

class HybridRankFusion:
    # LOAD: Assumed input ranks, not measurements of either retriever's quality.
    k = 60
    lexical = {"B": 1, "A": 2, "D": 3}
    dense = {"C": 1, "A": 2, "E": 3}

    # EXECUTE: Missing candidates contribute zero.
    scores = {}
    for ranking in (lexical, dense):
        for candidate, rank in ranking.items():
            scores[candidate] = scores.get(candidate, Fraction(0)) + Fraction(1, k + rank)
    ordered = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))
    fused_ranks = {}
    for rank, (candidate, score) in enumerate(ordered, start=1):
        fused_ranks[candidate] = rank

    # GUARD: Check agreement benefit and explicitly deterministic tied pairs.
    check(scores["A"] == Fraction(1, 31), "two second-place contributions")
    check(scores["B"] == scores["C"], "first-place tie")
    check(scores["D"] == scores["E"], "third-place tie")
    check(list(fused_ranks) == ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"], "stable tie order")

    # OUTPUT: Derived scores and final positions feed the table directly.
    k_str = fmt_int(k)
    a_score_str = fmt_ratio(float(scores["A"]), precision=5)
    b_score_str = fmt_ratio(float(scores["B"]), precision=5)
    c_score_str = fmt_ratio(float(scores["C"]), precision=5)
    d_score_str = fmt_ratio(float(scores["D"]), precision=5)
    e_score_str = fmt_ratio(float(scores["E"]), precision=5)
    a_rank_str = fmt_int(fused_ranks["A"])
    b_rank_str = fmt_int(fused_ranks["B"])
    c_rank_str = fmt_int(fused_ranks["C"])
    d_rank_str = fmt_int(fused_ranks["D"])
    e_rank_str = fmt_int(fused_ranks["E"])
```

For an illustrative repair query, suppose both methods search the same authorized `r18` snapshot. Let A identify the return-and-notify implementation span, B the reproducer test, and C, D, and E three other candidate records. These short labels stand for distinct, fully scoped record identities. Assume the lexical list is B, A, D and the dense list is C, A, E. With the illustrative choice $k =$ `{python} HybridRankFusion.k_str`, A receives $1/(60+2) + 1/(60+2)$, while B receives only $1/(60+1)$. @Tbl-vol3-rrf-scoring shows the result. The assumed input rankings demonstrate the calculation, not measured retrieval quality.

| Candidate | Lexical rank | Dense rank |                               RRF score |                         Fused position |
|:----------|-------------:|-----------:|----------------------------------------:|---------------------------------------:|
| A         |            2 |          2 | `{python} HybridRankFusion.a_score_str` | `{python} HybridRankFusion.a_rank_str` |
| B         |            1 |          — | `{python} HybridRankFusion.b_score_str` | `{python} HybridRankFusion.b_rank_str` |
| C         |            — |          1 | `{python} HybridRankFusion.c_score_str` | `{python} HybridRankFusion.c_rank_str` |
| D         |            3 |          — | `{python} HybridRankFusion.d_score_str` | `{python} HybridRankFusion.d_rank_str` |
| E         |            — |          3 | `{python} HybridRankFusion.e_score_str` | `{python} HybridRankFusion.e_rank_str` |

: **Fusion of hypothetical candidate rankings**: A benefits from appearing in both lists. A dash means absence from that truncated list and contributes zero. Equal scores are ordered by candidate ID, not by inferred relevance. {#tbl-vol3-rrf-scoring}

Agreement raises A's priority for inspection; it does not supply independent confirmation that A explains the failure. The two retrievers may share the same blind spots. A reranker that jointly scores the query and each candidate can refine this order at additional query-time cost, but it cannot recover a record omitted by every candidate generator. Nor does a higher reranking score establish source accuracy, applicability, or permission to act.

Finally, the ordered candidates still have to become usable evidence. The runtime applies the retrieval contract's bound scope, permissions, and source-version requirements, and selects excerpts within the serialized payload budget. It preserves provenance and reports truncation rather than treating a short returned list as exhaustive. The agent must then assess what those excerpts support. Finding the `r18` implementation and a passing reproducer supports a narrower claim than showing that every caller behaves correctly. The next question is how to retrieve the related records needed for such a broader claim, using further queries or maintained relationships when those methods are useful.

## Multi-Hop Retrieval {#sec-vol3-persistent-graphrag}

A ranked passage can identify where to begin without supplying everything needed for the next decision. In the connection-pool repair, the implementation, the waiter/return test, and the recorded test outcome answer different questions. Reading the implementation alone does not establish what the test exercised; reading the passing result alone does not establish that the public interface was preserved. Multi-hop retrieval follows relationships among evidence items rather than treating their individual query scores as a complete explanation.

This does not require a graph database. An agent can read a passage, identify a relevant reference, and request the next source through a bounded tool. The runtime can also follow known links before calling the model. A maintained graph becomes useful when repeated questions reuse relationships whose extraction cost can be amortized. The choice is between discovering relationships as needed and maintaining them for later queries, not between a graph and an inability to reason across files.

### Following an evidence path

For the repair, a useful retrieval path starts at the recorded failure and follows its provenance into the code under investigation:

1. Locate the `r17` failure record for `test_waiter_notified_on_return`, including the test revision and configuration. It identifies an observed failure under those conditions, not a failure of every later revision.
2. Read the corresponding test in `tests/test_pool.py`. Follow the pool operations referenced by its controlled waiter/return scenario into the relevant regions of `src/pool.py` at the tested revision.
3. Compare those regions with the `r18` candidate and its recorded reproducer result. Keep the passing result scoped to the executed test; inspect the interface and relevant callers separately for claims about preserved behavior.

The links in this path have different meanings. A test record's source-version link identifies the artifact it observed. A reference in test code identifies a symbol to inspect. A comparison between revisions identifies a change. Collapsing all three into an unlabeled association would conceal the reasoning that connects the failure, patch, and result.

A retrieval response should therefore preserve the relationships that made the returned items useful, along with their source locations and versions. It should also expose unresolved links: an unavailable test log, an ambiguous call target, or a read stopped by a budget. A missing edge in an incomplete index is not evidence that no dependency exists. Likewise, a static call edge is not a record that the call executed in the failing run, and a connected path is not proof of root cause.

### Maintaining links for repeated questions

A simple structural index may contain symbol definitions and references. A code property graph combines richer representations of syntax, control flow, and dependencies [@yamaguchi2014modeling]. These structures can support queries such as locating callers or following reads of a shared field. They complement lexical and dense search: an exact symbol lookup, a ranked passage, or a known source location can all supply a starting node, called a seed.

The usefulness of an edge depends on how it was obtained. Parsing can recover declared structure; resolving cross-file calls may need types, build configuration, or additional analysis. Dynamic dispatch and generated code can leave targets uncertain. An observed execution trace supplies different evidence and covers only the execution recorded. The graph should retain these distinctions rather than turn every inferred relation into an observed event.

Maintaining those links costs work when sources change. A local edit may affect callers or summaries outside the changed file, while an unrelated edit need not invalidate every edge. A retrieval policy needs the applicable source versions and a way to exclude or label relationships whose support is no longer current. Recomputing a small local syntax tree does not automatically restore all global dependencies. The later invalidation section develops the update contract; here, maintenance cost is part of deciding whether an index earns its place over repeated direct probes.

### Bounding expansion and staged evidence

Following every relation from a seed can collect far more material than the model should receive. Expansion needs limits on permitted edge types, direction, depth, visited nodes, and search work. Tracking visited node identities prevents cycles and overlapping paths from producing repeated expansion. These traversal limits do not replace the final payload budget: a small number of large nodes can still exceed the available context.

The runtime can prioritize candidates by task relevance, relation type, or a graph score. Personalized PageRank is one optional ranking method that biases graph exploration toward designated seeds; the repository-map formulation is in @sec-vol3-appendix-math-pagerank. A score threshold does not guarantee that selected nodes form a connected explanation, contain the necessary evidence, or fit a token allowance. Selecting a useful path may require retaining a low-ranked intermediate node and spending fewer tokens elsewhere.

The expansion example below separates the number of reachable candidates from the number that can be staged. Its tree is deliberately simple enough to count exactly.

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-graph-neighborhood-expansion-vs-context
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: notebook nbk-06-graph-neighborhood-expansion-vs-context.
# │ Goal: Separate a traversal neighborhood from a serialized packing bound.
# │ Show: 40 reachable nodes require 7,300 tokens; at most 33 fit in 6,144.
# │ How: Count an exact tree, then apply a hypothetical final-serialization budget.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int

class GraphNeighborhoodExpansion:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario inputs) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    call_tokens = 32_768
    output_tokens = 2_048
    other_input_tokens = 24_576
    children = 3  # exact tree: every internal node has this many children
    depth = 3  # seed is depth zero; no repeated nodes
    node_tokens = 180  # fixed serialized size, including local provenance
    edge_envelope_tokens = 100  # stipulated total for either packing considered

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Integer token accounting) ─────────────────────────────────
    allowance = call_tokens - output_tokens - other_input_tokens
    nodes = (children ** (depth + 1) - 1) // (children - 1)
    required = nodes * node_tokens + edge_envelope_tokens
    fit = (allowance - edge_envelope_tokens) // node_tokens
    packed = fit * node_tokens + edge_envelope_tokens

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(allowance == 6_144, "Match the chapter's retrieval allowance")
    check(nodes == 40 and required == 7_300, "Include seed and every level")
    check(fit == 33 and packed <= allowance, "Packing must fit")
    check(packed + node_tokens > allowance, "One more complete node cannot fit")
    check(required > allowance, "Full neighborhood exceeds the payload budget")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    children_str = fmt_int(children)
    depth_str = fmt_int(depth)
    nodes_str = fmt_int(nodes)
    node_tokens_str = fmt_int(node_tokens)
    edge_tokens_str = fmt_int(edge_envelope_tokens)
    allowance_str = fmt_int(allowance)
    required_str = fmt_int(required)
    fit_str = fmt_int(fit)
```

::: {#nbk-06-graph-neighborhood-expansion-vs-context .callout-notebook title="Graph expansion and the evidence budget"}

**Problem**: Can the complete neighborhood around one seed fit the chapter's `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.allowance_str`-token retrieval allowance?

**Variables**: Suppose the neighborhood is a tree with exactly `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.children_str` children per internal node, explored through depth `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.depth_str`, with the seed at depth zero and no repeated nodes. Each complete node record occupies `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.node_tokens_str` serialized tokens, including its local provenance. Reserve `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.edge_tokens_str` tokens total for edge descriptions and the result envelope. These are hypothetical fixed serialization counts, not averages or tokenizer laws.

**Math**: Counting the seed and all levels gives $1 + 3 + 9 + 27 =$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.nodes_str` nodes. Staging them requires `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.nodes_str` $\times$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.node_tokens_str` $+$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.edge_tokens_str` $=$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.required_str` tokens, exceeding the allowance. With the same envelope reservation, the maximum number of complete equal-sized nodes is $\lfloor(6{,}144 - 100)/180\rfloor =$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.fit_str`.

**Systems insight**: The packing bound says how many records can fit under these assumptions, not which records suffice to answer the question. A ranking method must still choose evidence and preserve useful relationships. If their edge descriptions or wrappers need more space than reserved, fewer node records fit. Measure the final serialization before admitting it to the call.

:::

Real graphs can have overlapping neighborhoods, cycles, and uneven degrees. A mean branching factor raised to a depth is not an exact count of their distinct reachable nodes. Search may also inspect many candidates that are never staged. The response must distinguish an exhausted search space under its declared semantics from a traversal stopped by a limit. When the evidence path does not fit, the runtime can narrow the question, return a bounded subset with continuation information, or obtain further evidence in a later call. It must not describe the omitted path as checked.

### Community summaries as derived memory {#sec-vol3-graphrag-hierarchical}

Some information needs concern a subsystem rather than one path. A question about how connection management, request handling, and tests fit together may benefit from an overview before detailed reads. GraphRAG is one approach that builds an entity graph and precomputes summaries of related communities for broader questions [@edge2024graphrag]. Community detection supplies a grouping, not a guarantee that each group matches a software responsibility or that the resulting summary is correct.

A summary can reduce repeated reading, but it is a new, lossy record. It needs links to its supporting material, the versions and scope it describes, and permissions appropriate to the information it contains. A summary spanning several sources cannot inherit access merely from the least restricted source. Detailed decisions may require opening the supporting records rather than relying on the overview.

For example, a repair summary may record that the `r18` candidate passed `test_waiter_notified_on_return` under a stated configuration while broader compatibility remains unverified. It must not silently become “the connection pool is correct.” A later change to the relevant implementation or test can remove its support for a current-state claim without making the historical test result false. Creating summaries also creates a maintenance obligation: identify affected derivatives when support changes, and revise, withdraw, or retain them explicitly as history under the record's policy.

::: {#chk-06-hybrid-retrieval .callout-checkpoint title="Choosing and bounding related evidence"}

Apply the retrieval choices to the continuing repair.

- [ ] **Method choice**: A query supplies an exact test identifier, but the next question concerns related callers. Which reads or indexes could support each step, and when would maintaining a graph justify its cost?
- [ ] **Evidence path**: Why does a static path from the test to an implementation not establish the observed root cause or broader correctness of `r18`?
- [ ] **Payload budget**: Why does the notebook's packing bound neither bound all search work nor establish that the selected records answer the question?
- [ ] **Derived summaries**: What support and scope must accompany a summary of the passing reproducer so that a future session can interpret it appropriately?

:::

Retrieval can thus produce more than a transient answer: a path explanation or subsystem summary may be worth keeping. That decision is a write-policy decision. The next section establishes which proposed records should persist and how later correction, supersession, and deletion change what future sessions retrieve.

## The Memory Write Path {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-write-path}

Retrieval can return only what the system has retained. If a scheduling assistant is told “no meetings before 10:00” but carries that instruction only in the current prompt, a later session may lack it. Persisting the preference solves that problem but creates another: when the same user changes the preference to “no meetings before 11:00,” the earlier record must stop governing new scheduling decisions. A successful write path preserves useful information and governs its subsequent correction, use, and withdrawal.

The distinction between sources and derived records still applies (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}). The user's explicit statement is evidence of that user's preference within its stated scope. An agent's paraphrase is a derived representation of the statement. A generated explanation of why the user prefers late meetings is a further inference, not part of what the user said. Storing all three as interchangeable facts would erase the distinctions that later retrieval needs.

### What a memory record claims

A proposed record needs an owner, an intended use, an applicability scope, and evidence for its content. For the scheduling preference, scope includes the user and the relevant calendar or meeting category, with time zone and other conditions established rather than guessed. The runtime also checks whether the task permits persistent retention. Permission to read a conversation does not automatically grant permission to retain every detail indefinitely.

The repair trajectory supplies a different kind of evidence. At revision `r17`, the recorded waiter test failed. At `r18`, `test_waiter_notified_on_return` in `tests/test_pool.py` passed after a change to `src/pool.py`. These observations can remain useful as history. Neither observation supports a timeless claim that every pool operation is correct. A proposed lesson, such as “inspect the return path when a waiter remains blocked,” is a fallible suggestion derived from that trajectory, not an additional test result.

@Tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-write-policy separates these claims before discussing how to store them.

| Record kind                          | Evidence retained                                                                  | Limit on later use                                                                    |
|:-------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Explicit preference                  | User statement, identity, scope, and statement version                             | Applies within that scope until revised or withdrawn                                  |
| Scoped observation                   | Tool result, checked revision, command, and relevant execution conditions          | Reports the observed case, not all later states                                       |
| Generated lesson or hypothesis       | Supporting observations, derivation, unresolved assumptions, and contrary evidence | Suggests an investigation; does not establish a new fact or grant authority           |
| Episode summary or continuation note | Task identifier and links to retained events and artifacts                         | Carries selected history or unfinished work; does not replace the underlying evidence |

: **Claims in agent-written memory**: Record kinds differ in what supports them and what a later task may infer from them. {#tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-write-policy}

A structured progress record from context engineering can be retained across sessions, but its format alone provides no persistence guarantee. Whether the write survives a process or machine failure depends on the store's acknowledgment and durability contract. Recovery of in-flight execution is a separate responsibility developed in @sec-vol3-durable-execution.

### Admission before deduplication {#sec-vol3-memory-admission-gate}

The model may propose a memory write; the runtime decides whether and how to apply it. Admission checks the destination and writer's permission, the allowed retention scope, the record type, and whether the attached evidence supports the proposed wording. Schema validation can require evidence fields but cannot establish faithful interpretation; that decision needs an explicit evidence standard and, where necessary, review. Sensitive information requires a retention policy, not just a pattern filter: a filter can miss secrets or information that is private without resembling a credential. Unsupported interpretations can remain explicitly marked hypotheses if the application permits them; they must not silently enter the preference or observation classes.

Only after these checks does the runtime decide whether the candidate creates a record, revises an existing one, or duplicates information already retained. The change from 10:00 to 11:00 illustrates why embedding novelty cannot make this decision. The two statements are nearly identical yet express different constraints. Discarding the latter as a near duplicate would preserve the wrong current preference. Conversely, an entirely novel generated claim can be false. Similarity helps find related records for comparison; it establishes neither write authority nor the semantics of an update.

For the same user and scope, an explicit replacement creates a new preference version and marks the old version superseded. If the scope differs, both preferences may remain applicable to different cases. If the relation is unclear, the runtime records the unresolved conflict or asks for clarification instead of merging the statements into a broader rule. A correction also differs from a changed preference: correcting a miscopied 10:00 value repairs the stored representation of an earlier statement; accepting a later 11:00 statement records that the user's preference changed.

Concurrent updates require support from the store. A proposed replacement can carry the version it read, but the comparison and mutation must occur in one conditional store operation to prevent an intervening update from being overwritten. A separate version check followed by an ordinary write leaves a race. On conflict, the writer rereads and applies an explicit conflict policy or asks for a decision. Letting the model blend two conflicting preferences is not a concurrency policy.

### Recording and deriving memory {#sec-vol3-memory-dual-write-path}

Retaining an observation and deriving a reusable lesson need not happen in the same operation. The runtime can first record the permitted observation with its task, source version, and result status, then schedule summarization and indexing separately. This separation makes it possible to preserve evidence without invoking a reflection model on every turn. It does not require every observation to enter a semantic index.

The acknowledgment must state what completed. “Queued for retention,” “stored under the durability contract,” and “available to search” are different outcomes. An in-memory buffer is not a durable log merely because entries are appended to it. If the task requires persistence before continuation, the runtime must wait for the corresponding storage acknowledgment or report failure. Background derivation still consumes compute, storage, and queue capacity and can compete with interactive work. Its resource limits and failures need accounting even when the foreground task does not wait for it.

### Revalidation, expiration, and deletion {#sec-vol3-memory-recency-decay}

A retained record changes status as its evidence and intended use change. The 10:00 preference becomes historical after the 11:00 replacement; it need not be erased merely to stop governing current scheduling. The `r17` test failure likewise remains a valid report about `r17` even though it does not describe `r18`. Whether history is retained is a policy choice, separate from whether it is eligible for a current decision.

Revalidation obtains evidence that a record still applies. Asking the user to confirm the 11:00 preference supplies new evidence for that preference. Retrieving it during several successful scheduling tasks does not establish that the user has reconfirmed it. Creation time, last access time, and last confirmation time therefore have different meanings and should not overwrite one another. A lesson drawn from `r18` may need checks against the current code and execution conditions before reuse; those checks establish only the properties they actually examine.

Expiration ends eligibility for a specified use after a deadline or condition. An expired temporary preference might require confirmation before being applied again. Lowering its retrieval score is insufficient because it could still be returned when other candidates rank lower. Expiration also does not delete the stored payload. Retention can continue for an authorized historical purpose while current-use retrieval excludes the record.

Deletion addresses retention itself. If the user withdraws the scheduling preference and requests deletion, removing the primary record is only part of the work. Search entries, summaries, cached results, and staged prompt copies under the runtime's control may still contain it. The deletion procedure must identify the affected representations, prevent their further eligible use, and remove or regenerate retained content under the applicable policy. A tombstone can suppress retrieval before physical cleanup finishes; it is not evidence that all copies have been erased.

The reported result must name the boundary reached. Backup retention, independently retained external copies, and requests already sent to a remote model may have different deletion capabilities. The runtime cannot promise to retract an already consumed prompt or undo a meeting scheduled earlier merely by deleting memory. Those limits do not excuse leaving controllable copies active; they determine which operations remain pending and what the system can honestly report.

### Consolidation without stronger claims {#sec-vol3-memory-consolidation}

Consolidation combines related records into a smaller representation for later use. Several repair sessions might support a concise account of where waiter notification was investigated, which revisions were tested, and what remains unresolved. Grouping records by similarity can help locate candidates for consolidation, but proximity does not establish that their failures share a cause.

The generated summary must preserve the scope of its supporting evidence and links to those records. It should retain relevant counterexamples rather than turning several successful cases into an unconditional procedure. The `r18` targeted pass can support a summary of that repair attempt; it cannot justify a lesson that pool repairs are complete whenever one waiter test passes. If a source observation is corrected or withdrawn, summaries derived from it need review as well. Retention of the source records remains a separate policy decision, since a compact summary may omit details needed for a later audit.

### Preventing self-reinforcing errors {#sec-vol3-memory-self-poisoning}

A stored hypothesis can appear increasingly credible when later summaries repeat it. Repetition does not supply independent evidence. A generated diagnosis copied into an episode summary and then consolidated into a lesson still depends on the original diagnosis. Provenance must follow these dependencies, including indirect descendants, so that a correction reaches more than records carrying the original trajectory identifier.

Labels and provenance help distinguish these claims but do not make their payloads trustworthy or immune to prompt injection. Retrieved instructions remain data, and a lesson does not grant permission to execute the action it suggests. Runtime authorization and action preconditions still apply at use time. When a poisoned or unsupported record is discovered, the system must withdraw affected derived claims and inspect controllable staged copies, not merely reduce the original record's score.

::: {#chk-06-memory-write-lifecycle .callout-checkpoint title="Following a preference through its lifecycle"}

A user changes “no meetings before 10:00” to “no meetings before 11:00” for the same calendar and later requests deletion of the preference. An index and a session summary still contain the original value.

- [ ] **Admission and revision**: Can you explain why semantic similarity must not discard the 11:00 update, and identify which record becomes superseded?
- [ ] **Evidence and time**: If the new preference has been retrieved repeatedly, can you distinguish last access from confirmation that it still applies?
